title: Adaptive stitching and tenant-aware prefix cache review - Sapphire AI
summary: Medium-depth technical review of prefix/prompt caching strategy. Discussed adaptive stitching, tenant-scoped keys, eviction, hit-rate telemetry, and safety for multi-tenant shared caches. Reviewed tradeoffs for Dedicated vs Private (VPC/on-prem), batching/quantization impacts, and next steps for a pilot and benchmark run.
topics: adaptive stitching and partial prefix reuse
batching & quantization impact on cache effectiveness
next_steps: Redwood to share cached-keying design doc and sample key schemas
Sapphire to provide 2 weeks of request traces (anonymized) for hit-rate simulation
Schedule on-prem pilot plan review for week of Dec 8
Marco to run a micro-benchmark comparing KV hit-rate vs latency with quantized LLMs and share results
action_items: Marco Chen: produce key-pattern simulation and sample scripts by 2025-11-27
Priya Nair: export anonymized prompt traces (s3 link) by 2025-11-25
Lina Park: circulate security checklist and Redwood Private packaging options by 2025-11-24
transcript:
[00:00] Lina Park: hey everyone good morning, thanks for joining. i'm lina from redwood, i'll kick us off. we got marco here who will do the deep bits.
[00:12] Priya Nair: morning, thanks. we've been looking at prefix reuse and thought it made sense to get a sanity check on a multi-tenant strategy before we start a pilot.
[00:23] Marco Chen: cool. quick agenda — current workload profile, proposed keying patterns, adaptive stitching idea, eviction/ttl, hit-rate telemetry, then open q&a. sound okay?
[00:36] Jonas Meyer: yes fine. quick note — our traffic is 60% short support queries (avg 60 tokens) and 40% long generation, lots of common prefixes for prompts like product intros.
[00:52] Eliot Ramos: infra constraint — we want to run under our VPC for data residency, possibly on-prem for PHI. so any caching must be controllable in private mode.
[01:06] Marco Chen: understood. first slide — keying basics. we recommend a layered key: model-version|tokenized-prefix-hash|tenant-id|schema-version. that gives you fast equality checks but still tenant-aware.
[01:25] Marta Duque: curious — why tenant-id in the key and not separate namespace? could be cost in memory if we shard per tenant.
[01:33] Marco Chen: good q. we considered both. adding tenant-id to the key lets a single shared cache enforce logical isolation without physical siloing, reducing memory overhead. downside: risk of collisions if hashing is weak and more variance in hit-rate across tenants.
[01:52] Priya Nair: are there cases where shared cache leaks prompts across tenants? compliance team flagged that as a hard no.
[01:59] Marco Chen: if you include tenant-id in the key, you won't merge outputs across tenants. the larger risk is in side-channel inference when hit behaviour is observable — we can reduce that with constant-time eviction reporting and masked telemetry.
[02:16] Priya Nair: hmm, walk me through adaptive stitching — that was a new term for our team.
[02:21] Marco Chen: sure. adaptive stitching is where we store cached KV states for prefix segments — e.g., first 64 tokens, then 128 tokens — and at request time we try to stitch the longest matching contiguous prefix. it allows partial reuse for prompts that vary slightly.
[02:39] Jonas Meyer: so if user prompt adds a one-line context, we'd still reuse the earlier prefix?
[02:44] Marco Chen: exactly. instead of only exact-match keys, we keep segment-level entries and a small stitching table. in practice we've seen 20–40% improvement in effective hit-rate on conversational apps.
[02:58] Lina Park: note — the stitching table itself is small metadata; we prefer a bloom-filter like structure to quickly rule out misses.
[03:08] Eliot Ramos: my worry — stitching seems stateful and could complicate multi-node coherence in Dedicated pools.
[03:16] Marco Chen: good point. for Dedicated we run a central metadata service for stitching plus eventual consistency of segments. for Private/on-prem we can colocate cache metadata with inference nodes to avoid cross-VPC calls. that was what we meant by cache locality.
[03:34] Priya Nair: any numbers on latency penalty for stitching?
[03:38] Marco Chen: typically +2–6 ms on the critical path if it's local; if we need a metadata RPC across AZs it can be +10–30 ms. those are rough; depends on network. that's why we recommend colocated metadata in VPC/on-prem pilots.
[03:55] Jonas Meyer: and what about batching? when we batch, does stitching still help or do we lose granularity?
[04:02] Marco Chen: batching can coalesce similar prefixes, which actually increases chance of reuse. but large batches increase tail latency. our runtime does adaptive batching: it favors small tail-latency SLOs for interactive routes and larger batch sizes for background generation. stitching and batching are complementary.
[04:19] Priya Nair: quantization — i guess compressed weights change runtimes. Does that impact cache semantics?
[04:25] Marco Chen: semantically no, the model outputs are the same up to quantization error. practically, different quantization profiles may yield slightly different logits and KV structures. we version cache entries by model-quantization-tag so you don't mix 8-bit vs 4-bit results.
[04:40] Marta Duque: can cache keys include prompt metadata like zero-shot vs few-shot?
[04:45] Marco Chen: yes we add a small metadata fingerprint that captures prompt template id and sampling params (temp/beam). Leaves deterministic responses in cache. sampling non-determinism is not safe to cache unless you deteminize or tag.
[04:59] Lina Park: an oft-misunderstood point — caching is best for deterministic paths (e.g., system prompts) and prefix-heavy workloads. For user-facing creative generation we often rely less on caching.
[05:14] Priya Nair: our legal team requires proof we never return text from other tenants. you said tenant in key prevents that, but are there additional mitigations?
[05:23] Marco Chen: yes: tenant-id in key prevents cross-tenant retrieval. on top, we support optional per-tenant isolation modes: logical (shared cache with tenant key), physical (per-tenant cache instance), and hybrid (hot-shard per-tenant plus shared cold pool). we can show memory vs cost tradeoff.
[05:42] Jonas Meyer: what's hybrid hot-shard look like?
[05:46] Marco Chen: you reserve N entries per tenant for hot prefixes (e.g., 10k) in a fast LRU cache, and a global shared pool handles long-tail keys. hot-shard ensures your top prompts stay siloed.
[05:57] Priya Nair: eviction — LRU or TTL?
[06:01] Marco Chen: both. We do TTL for time-based expiry and LRU for capacity. we also support custom eviction hooks so you can pin keys programmatically.
[06:10] Jonas Meyer: how do you measure hit-rate and attribute it to tenant behaviour vs general model popularity?
[06:16] Marco Chen: we instrument per-key telemetry: key hash, tenant, model-version, hit/miss counts, and approximate frequency buckets. to protect privacy we sample and aggregate. we recommend an SLI: rolling 7-day effective reuse ratio and per-route tail latency.
[06:31] Eliot Ramos: sounds telemetry-heavy — any compliance concerns?
[06:35] Lina Park: telemetry can be anonymized before leaving VPC; for Private deployments all telemetry stays in-customer network unless they opt-in.
[06:44] Priya Nair: pilot plan — we can give traces but we want a simulation run first. can you run a hit-rate simulation on our trace to estimate cost savings?
[06:53] Marco Chen: yes. we have a simulator that replays tokenized traces against keying policies and stitching heuristics. if you share 2 weeks of anonymized traces we can return a hit-rate forecast and a shadow latency distribution.
[07:08] Marta Duque: any risks with prefix hash collisions?
[07:12] Marco Chen: collisions are low if you use 128-bit hashes; worst case you detect mismatch at KV level by storing a short verification fingerprint. collisions in practice negligible but we include fallback to rerun from scratch if mismatch.
[07:25] Priya Nair: developer ergonomics — how do engineers mark which parts of the prompt are cacheable?
[07:30] Marco Chen: we expose a small SDK: annotate prompt segments with cacheable=true, provide template ids, and optionally compute a canonicalized prefix before sending. also we auto-detect repeated system prompts.
[07:44] Jonas Meyer: what's the per-token savings in cost?
[07:48] Marco Chen: depends on hit-rate. at 30% effective reuse you can see 20–35% token cost reduction overall due to KV caching avoiding decoder compute. with stitching we often bump that effective reuse to 40–55% in repeat-heavy flows.
[08:04] Eliot Ramos: in Dedicated mode, if we have reserved gpus, does caching change scheduling?
[08:09] Marco Chen: yes — cached requests skip some compute stages and can be routed to lower-tier nodes or CPU-offload endpoints, which reduces GPU utilization. that's a policy — you can pin cached hits to cheaper worker pools.
[08:21] Priya Nair: on-prem PHI case — is there support for HSM/KMS for key wrapping?
[08:27] Marco Chen: yes. customer-managed KMS/HSM for secrets is supported in Private; cache encryption at rest is supported with KMS keys. logs and their keys remain in customer control in Private.
[08:40] Lina Park: quick interjection — i saw a question in chat from Marta about bloom filter false positive rates.
[08:46] Marta Duque: yeah, if bloom filter says a prefix exists but it's actually false, we may try to fetch and miss — what's your mitigation?
[08:53] Marco Chen: we size the bloom filter to keep fp < 0.1%. false positives cause an extra fetch but not correctness issues. plus we have a fallback fast negative cache to avoid repeated wasted probes.
[09:06] Priya Nair: how about cost model — do you charge for cache hits differently?
[09:11] Lina Park: generally usage-based billing still counts tokens served but cached responses can be billed at a lower compute unit because they bypass heavy GPU compute. for Dedicated it's part of your reserved util and reduces effective consumption.
[09:24] Jonas Meyer: security review point — audit logs for cache reads/writes? need to show who accessed cached items and when.
[09:31] Marco Chen: we log cache operations with tenant id and operation type; for Private it's local logs you control. we can add redaction or sampling.
[09:40] Priya Nair: curious — are there attack vectors where an attacker could spam prefixes to evict others?
[09:46] Marco Chen: yes cache poisoning/eviction attacks are a concern. mitigation: per-tenant quotas, request rate limits, and weighted eviction where tenant hot-shards are protected. also rate-limited creation of new heavy entries and anomaly detection in access patterns.
[10:02] Marta Duque: do you support TTL slippage per tenant? some tenants need longer retention.
[10:07] Marco Chen: yes per-tenant policies for TTL and reserved hot capacity. the tradeoff is global memory footprint.
[10:15] Priya Nair: for the simulation run, what format do you need the traces in?
[10:20] Marco Chen: tokenized JSON lines with timestamp, tenant id (anonymized), model-version, prompt_text, route. we provide a small converter script.
[10:30] Jonas Meyer: ok. about stitching metadata consistency — if we colocate metadata on each inference node how do we handle evictions across nodes?
[10:38] Marco Chen: we use a lightweight gossip protocol for hot-shard counters and a central reconciliation job that runs every 30s. consistency is eventual; for hot shards we keep a small sticky allocation to ensure correctness.
[10:50] Lina Park: quick practical: for your pilot, we recommend starting with logical tenant keying + hot-shard for top 10 tenants, run simulator, then decide if we need physical siloing.
[11:00] Priya Nair: sounds reasonable. timeline?
[11:03] Lina Park: Marco estimates simulator results in 3–5 business days after trace receipt. then a 2-week pilot to validate in VPC.
[11:11] Priya Nair: ok we'll pick two tenant cohorts — support chat and marketing copy generation.
[11:16] Eliot Ramos: one final nit — are you able to run the cache metadata service inside our VPC?
[11:21] Marco Chen: yes in Private we deploy all control plane components into your VPC or on-prem. for Dedicated we can also run a customer-controlled metadata tier.
[11:31] Jonas Meyer: any gotchas with quantized models and KV size?
[11:35] Marco Chen: quantization may reduce KV footprint slightly because less precise activations compress better; but in our profiling KV size is dominated by embeddings and keying metadata, so impact modest.
[11:46] Marta Duque: request — can you include a section in the design doc on instrumentation naming conventions? our infra team wants to map to prometheus metrics easily.
[11:54] Lina Park: noted, we'll add prometheus-friendly metric names + grafana dashboards for the pilot.
[12:00] Priya Nair: ok let's recap and next steps.
[12:04] Lina Park: recap: redwood to run simulator on provided traces; share keying design doc and SDK snippets; pilot plan for VPC on-prem options; security checklist.
[12:14] Marco Chen: action: i will run a micro-benchmark comparing 8-bit vs 4-bit quantized runtimes and how hit-rate interacts with batch sizing — deliver by next thursday.
[12:26] Priya Nair: thanks everyone. schedule follow-up for Dec 9 to review pilot results?
[12:31] Lina Park: yes i'll send a calendar invite after the call. thanks all.
[12:36] (meeting ends)
note: Transcript contains occasional transcription artifacts: 'K V cash' instead of KV cache, 'Privy' for Private in a few spots. Kept natural speech patterns and interruptions.
